judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the final version of Senate Bill 69. Lawsuit-funding companies must register, avoid certain foreign ties, and cannot control cases, pay referral fees, use false ads, or collect more than the plaintiff after legal costs. Contracts need written disclosures and cancellation terms; funding is open to court discovery, funders of $25,000 or more may share costs for baseless cases, and seat-belt evidence is allowed. The Georgia House agreed 120-42, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the final version of Senate Bill 40. Scrap dealers may pay at most $100 cash and make at most two daily deals per seller; no cash is allowed for listed converters, coils, wires, copper, or batteries. It expands converter records and a recycler registry, splits each $200 fee into $100 for the sheriffs and $100 for the county, and adds shredded vehicle or appliance waste to a local $1-per-ton disposal charge. The Georgia House agreed 91-63, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's version of House Bill 121. Each school campus must have an armed peace officer during school hours, but a district with a good reason may use a trained, armed school worker or guard instead. When a special education student is checked for danger, someone who knows the disability must join and serious violence risks must be reported at once; state safety money may pay for guards, safer buildings, and suicide prevention. The bill became law after the Texas House accepted the Senate's version 97-38.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on accepting the Senate's changes to House Bill 173. The Ohio House agreed 56-35, and the bill went to the governor. The bill covered companies that resell electric service to tenants and condominium owners through a building's own meters, called submetering. It took those companies out of the state's legal definition of a public utility. They would no longer be regulated by the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio. The Senate version still made them register with the commission, file compliance plans, and bill tenants at least 3 percent below the electric utility's own rate. The House had passed its own version 74-23 in March 2026. The governor vetoed the bill on June 24, 2026, so none of it took effect.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the final version of House Bill 463. It cuts personal tax from 5.19 percent to 4.99 percent in 2026, raises yearly cuts from 0.10 to 0.125 points, lowers their floor from 4.99 to 3.99 percent, and cuts business taxes. It raises exemptions from $4,000 to $5,000 and $12,000 to $15,000, excludes $1,750 of overtime and $1,750 of tips, raises the age-65 retirement break, and ends listed vehicle, data-center, and computer tax breaks. The Georgia House agreed 104-71, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the final version of House Bill 1185. Corporate rules may require internal company claims, including shareholder disclosure and records-inspection cases, to be heard only in Georgia's statewide business court. It allows moving those cases there and awarding legal fees and costs, with listed exceptions. The Georgia House agreed 97-65, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the final House-Senate deal on Senate Bill 37. Public college boards must review basic required courses every five years and may reverse course changes or some senior hires. Only boards may create faculty senates, which can only give advice; a governor-chosen official handles college complaints. The bill became law after the Texas House approved it 83-47.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the final version of Senate Bill 220. It allows medical cannabis as vapor, oil, or raw plant; replaces the 5 percent THC cap with 1,200 milligrams per package; and adds most cancers, bowel disease, HIV, and lupus. Patients may name adult or medical caregivers, public ads are barred but provider information is allowed, smoking stays illegal while vapor is allowed, and cards last five years, with electronic cards depending on funding. The Georgia Senate agreed 38-14, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the final version of Senate Bill 244. Counties pay reasonable defense costs when prosecutor misconduct causes removal and dismissal; wrongfully imprisoned people may file an innocence claim after reversal, cancellation, or pardon and prove it more likely than not. A state fund pays $75,000 per prison year, $25,000 per death-row year, legal fees, returned fines and restitution, and reentry and health costs. The Georgia Senate agreed 35-18, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the final version of Senate Bill 472. For districts under top financial monitoring or faulted for mismanagement, the state board may seek paid suspension of local board members, limit superintendent renewals to 12 months, and allow firing for cause. Extra state advances are capped at 50 percent of last year's funding without an auditor plan, and every local system and state charter school needs yearly financial and compliance audits. The Georgia Senate agreed 29-17, and it became law.
